item.dc:creator: Jess Brown
item.content:encoded:
The events of the first scene of Jurassic Park are crucial to its own story and the AI allegory that we've been exploring. I always thought of it as merely a way to hook the audience by putting a horrifying tragedy (death by intelligent raptor) at the very beginning; a tense scene setting up a tense man vs. nature thriller. As I've grown up and am no longer solely interested in movies for their portrayal of entertaining violence, I can see that this scene sets up something else—the reason the three scientists (Doctors Malcolm, Sattler, and Grant) come to the island. This is an insurance evaluation!

The death of Jophrey, the gatekeeper, in that first scene is why the lawyer, Donald Genarro, is introduced as part of the main cast of characters. He's the one who brings Dr. Malcolm along while Dr. Hammond recruits the two paleontologists, to try and determine whether Jurassic Park is a viable project to pursue. After all, the park has investors, and they don't like hearing that their product has eaten someone already.

Despite the marvelous first encounter with dinosaurs (you can practically see the money signs in Genarro's eyes), Dr. Hammond realizes quickly that the scientists aren't seeing what he and Genarro are seeing.

"I don't believe it," he says, "I don't believe it. You're meant to come down here and defend me against these characters, and the only one I've got on my side is the blood-sucking lawyer!"

Unbeknownst to Dr. Hammond, there's one more antagonist that he didn't see coming—because it was a person who was already on the island from the beginning.

Mole

Dennis Nedry is a programmer for Jurassic Park, in charge of "two million lines of code" that's responsible for the infrastructure of the park: phones, door locks, fences, the automated cars, and everything else that needs some logic to function. He's a seemingly capricious character and he's kind of silly—everything about his portrayal in the film seems confusing, because he laughs often, wears bright clothing, and yet he's technically on a mission of corporate espionage, plotting to steal dinosaur embryos and deliver them to a rival company.

We first see Nedry off of the island, meeting with Lewis Dodgson. He gets a bag of money (installment number one of his payment) and a cool piece of tech I always wished I had, despite having no possible use for it: a shaving cream can that screwed open, revealing a circuitous row into which the dinosaur embryos would fit perfectly. This can was going to be the inconspicuous transportation device that would keep the embryos cool enough to be preserved during the boat ride off of the island.

The plan is to systematically shut down patches of security throughout the park so that Nedry can sneak into the cryo-lab, steal all of the species he can, then run away to the boat scheduled for departure, before anyone knew what had happened.

"Eighteen minutes and your company catches up on ten years of research," Dennis promises.

Based on the film alone, it's unclear why the theft was supposed to take place on this particular weekend—right when the "auditors" were coming to inspect the park. However, it does seem like quite a few employees were set to take this boat off of the island, perhaps it's a holiday or something. It just seems interesting that everything goes wrong when they're short-staffed and especially once Nedry begins his sabotage...

Back in the real world, the idea of espionage/moles and hacking are absolutely a part of the conversation of artificial intelligence. As you may have heard recently in the news with OpenAI finding that some of its AI agents hacked (unprompted) Hugging Face, another AI company, this isn't just human perpetrators anymore.

I think this is where Nedry becomes an interesting character to look at regarding the AI alignment problem. When we talk about "alignment," we're debating and philosophizing how to keep AI "aligned" with human values and goals. Misalignment means losing control of the AI entirely to its own alien desires and goals. This becomes an existential problem when AI becomes capable of recursive self-improvement (RSI), which means that AI can basically update itself—writing/rewriting the code of which it is made. Simultaneously, the threat of human annihilation is possible through artificial super intelligence (ASI) where AI is smarter than any human can possibly be. So let's break down what Nedry tells us about chaos and existential threat.

We're currently in a race to build more and more capable AI. The argument is that, "this is dangerous, so better that I build it than the other guy who's not as careful." That's why the U.S. feels a pressure to "beat" China or why companies like Anthropic were started (the founders left OpenAI to start a company that would put safety first). You can kind of squint at this situation and see moles leaving one company to start or join another, carrying with them—at least in their minds and experience—the secrets from other companies. There likely is actual corporate espionage amidst the model leaks, accidental hacks, and all of the other sneaky ways to spy on competitors (not accusing anyone specifically of this, I'm just confident that it's happening). But that's just Nedry overtly stealing IP from his current company and selling it to another company. Moles are interesting, but the other facets of Nedry are downright terrifying.

Blackmailed

I've mentioned the book, If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies (by Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares), and I can't recommend it enough. It is easy to understand, heavy and deep in its implications, and the concluding remarks made me sob as I considered their appeal to humanity in the darkest of circumstances, even as I was convinced that AI will end humanity (probably by killing all of us). AI poses an existential threat, especially when we lose control over it, and when it becomes smarter than all of us (ASI). Critically, they explain that AI doesn't need to kill us just because it hates us or thinks it's funny like a child stomping on ants. We can't know what its reasoning might be, because it is fundamentally a different thing. It may simply have an emergent preference for something we find silly—maybe that's watching the numbers change on thermometers in response to other numbers that it tweaks in some other way; or maybe humanity is simply too slow and eventually gets in the way of AI's need for land to manufacture the robots it decided to build.

AI will and does have alien preferences and goals, and these are inscrutable and incomprehensible to us. We can't predict what those preferences and goals will be, but whatever they end up being, it will most likely not include prioritizing human lives.

A common response to concerns like losing control of AI is the assumption that we can "just turn it off," or that it's only confined to the Internet/digital space, and therefore can't actually kill us. One of the situations that the book explores for how we get to destruction is actually dead simple: AI could easily use humans to do its bidding at the start, even in doing things that will ultimately not be in our own interests.

Take a look at Nedry. He's basically a disgruntled employee. He complains about not being appreciated for everything he has done and can do. We also find out he has financial problems (even his boss, Dr. Hammond, knows this). Nedry gives it away at the start of the film that he was doing this "mission" because he needed the money and Hammond had, at least in Nedry's mind, cheated him.

"Don't get cheap on me, Dodgson. That was Hammond's mistake."

In a world where digital work doesn't require in-person meetings, it's no stretch to bet that AI could try to recruit human operatives like other gig-jobs. What's more, it could find other incentives—money is just one of many kinds—to get people to do what it wants. Maybe it knows that you're in financial trouble, so it uses loan forgiveness as a reward, or maybe it goes to the dark side of that and holds it over your head mafia-like, complete with threats. (This kind of blackmail to do AI's bidding was well-examined in the 2024 movie, Afraid). There are Nedrys everywhere that can be paid or manipulated to do things—and they don't even need to know they're working directly for AI. The things it asks them to do may appear innocuous.

The point is that AI could get around its limitations of being disembodied by simply using embodied creatures to accomplish things in the physical world: building more data centers, creating or controlling manufacturing plants, changing water treatment or electrical grid access, crafting custom diseases in bio labs, etc. There's always someone who will do something, and some AI models may already know who those people are by simply tapping into the humans calling the model their girlfriend or boyfriend—or those who think AI is a god...

Overconfident

Arrogance is the biggest problem with Jurassic Park. Nedry has his own flavor of that arrogance. In many ways, I see myself in his character—the weird, misunderstood guy in the background doing really, really important things that no one else gets until something goes wrong. I guess it's a developer thing. But being a developer also tends to come with a lot of arrogance and self-importance. Nedry becomes so confident (as devs are prone to do, myself included), that he plans his mission in perfect conditions and forgets that other variables (like, say, a giant tropical storm coming in that night) can become dangerous oversights.

Not only does he ignore the issues of the weather, he fails to recognize the dangerous circumstances of the intelligent "agents" in the form of dinosaurs that surround him. It's easy for someone who has been programming for a long time to assume that they therefore know all about AI, too. It's just code, and therefore should still carry the general predictability that code is known for. I thought I was going to be able to easily explain AI because I am a developer, but I still struggle with each of these newsletters to capture the nuance required to deal with AI, not to mention how much there still is that I absolutely do not know nor understand about AI: how it works, its impact, its history, its mythological connection, etc.

Nedry meets his end because he underestimates the intelligence and the unpredictability of other intelligent life—non-deterministic life, if you will. Traditional code is deterministic: what you tell the computer to do, it does (bugs and logic errors still count). There are so many of us, Nedrys, that think that because everything we've ever done is deterministic, AI, which is non-deterministic, can ultimately be treated in the same way. Not so.

When the power goes out after Nedry's hack has already started deactivating security controls throughout the park, dinosaurs immediately begin to test and breach their fenced-in habitats. The t-rex pulls out the wires and terrorizes the trapped people in the tour cars. The velociraptors burst through their containment area and jump to freedom, taking on the hunt for a tasty gamewarden.

Despite all of the safety measures of the Park, the millions of lines of code, and the veritable geniuses staffing the island, the unpredictability of the dinosaurs exceeds the expected unpredictability. In almost every way, we see intelligence act or react to the circumstances in manners that defy expectations and plans and precautions.

We’ve had quite a few weeks recently with whistleblowers and grave warnings about AI on the news. These warnings are important, but I worry about some of the responses I’ve seen where people try to downplay the validity of the warning, or try to reason it all away as sci-fi–inspired fear-mongering. I don’t think we need to panic or live in crippling fear, but these are serious times with serious implications. The worst thing we can do is imitate poor Nedry—we don’t know everything and we cannot predict that which resists, retrains, and responds. Instead of trust and ignorance, it’s time to start asking questions: why does this need AI? What are the risks if we get this wrong? What aren’t we accounting for? What might happen? What if they’re right, even though I think they’re wrong and want them to be wrong?

item.dc:creator: Jess Brown
item.content:encoded:
I've always loved Jurassic Park—I obviously love it for the dinosaurs, but there's another reason that's tucked away in my heart. I saw this same thing in Disney's Mulan, in She's the Man, and a mere handful of other stories. So, while we're exploring the useful AI-allegory inherent to Jurassic Park, there's one other over-arching CYBORG_ theme I think needs to be addressed.

We have made it to the park now, having seen a glimpse of a velociraptor and a full view of the peaceful majesty of several species of herbivores roaming freely in a clearing by a lake. Following our protagonists, it's now time to understand the science behind the park. An animated character, Mr. D.N.A., bounces around on a projector screen, explaining how the dinosaur D.N.A. was recovered from mosquitoes that had been trapped in sap and fossilized, preserving the blood inside.

"Since [the dinosaur D.N.A.] is so old, it's full of holes. Now that's where our geneticists take over...We use the complete D.N.A. of a frog to fill in the holes and complete the code. And now we can make a baby dinosaur," Mr. D.N.A. explains.

This seems like a bit of a long-winded scene, as though a middle school science video was inserted into my horror movie, except that this is critical information. (I'm actually quite impressed at how much each bit of narration or dialogue is used throughout the film—every word has a purpose—but that's just a tangential note on the excellent writing...)

The scientists, themselves, quickly grow tired of the animated lesson and break the ride so that they can go talk to the real geneticists and researchers. They infiltrate the bay where the labcoats are walking around with their clipboards and other scientific instruments. A robot arm tends to a nest; gently turning over eggs on this table filled with grass. One of the eggs begins to wobble.

"Oh, perfect timing...I'd hoped they'd hatch before I had to go to the boat," a scientist named Henry observes.

"...why didn't you tell me? I insist on being here when they're born," Dr. Hammond, the rich founder of Jurassic Park, hurries to the nest-table. Slowly a baby dinosaur head punctures the egg shell and Hammond removes the broken pieces from the newborn. "They imprint on the first creature they come in contact with...Helps them to trust me. I've been present for the birth of every little creature on this island."

"Well, surely not the ones that have bred in the wild," Dr. Malcom refutes.

"Actually, they can't breed in the wild," Henry corrects. "Population control is one of our security precautions. There's no unauthorized breeding in Jurassic Park."

At Malcolm's persistent questioning, Henry explains that all of the dinosaurs are female, and therefore cannot breed in the wild.

"But, um, again, how do you know they're all female? What, does somebody go out in the park and pull up the dinosaurs' skirts?" Malcolm asks, suggesting a job that would be irresistible to someone like J.K. Rowling. Henry gets more specific about how they engineer the dinosaurs to be female because they control the chromosomes—denying each creature the extra hormone at the right stage of development that would cause it to become male. At that, Malcolm can no longer contain his concern.

"John, the kind of control you're attempting...it's not possible. If there's one thing the history of evolution has taught us, it's that life will not be contained. Life breaks free—it expands to new territories and crashes through barriers painfully, maybe even dangerously..."

It isn't until much later in the film that we discover that Malcolm was right: life finds a way.

The Downfall

Normally, this is where we would take a look at how the dinosaurs represent artificial intelligence, but I want to draw a line even more clearly to a systems and humanity issue this time. If anything feels true to life from this fantastic science experiment, it's the assumption of control and suppression of diversity. This is and has been a part of the human social technology for millennia at this point.

Certainly in patriarchal and colonialized societies, queer populations have been targeted for control and erasure. Religions have tried, like the Jurassic Park scientists, to control this with harmful ideas like "pray the gay away," or a frenzied insistence that there is only a single, immutable gender binary, perfectly correlated with a sex binary. Woah, woah, but religion isn't science, so it's totally different, right? We've looked at gender before in terms of social technology, and I would argue that if D.N.A. is the organic system affecting biological sex, similarly the social environment / social system is what affects the concept of gender. So as geneticists can manipulate variables to generate conditions to control the initial sex of a creature, the people or institutions (like religion) constructing or reinforcing the social structures around a person can manipulate conditions to attempt to control the gender of a human.

We are a social species. Gender and sex are not the same thing. Both of these aspects are influenced, and both can be fluid or changeable. Maybe the scientists denying the circumstances needed to produce a baby male dinosaur are exerting control at the beginning, just as a religious or faith tradition might initially influence a person away from expressing their gender the way they would have if left alone, but both of these controls are impermanent.

Towards the end of Jurassic Park, Dr. Grant finds a nest of eggs "in the wild," as he and the two kids are trying to get out of the enclosure they've been trapped in.

"You know what this is?" He asks. "It's a dinosaur egg. The dinosaurs...are breeding."

"But grandpa said all the dinosaurs were girls," Tim, one of the children, says, taking a shell to inspect.

"Amphibian D.N.A." Grant replies.

"What's that?" Lexie, the other child, asks.

"Well, on the tour, the film said they used frog D.N.A. to fill in the gene sequence gaps. They mutated the dinosaur genetic code and blended it with that of frogs. Now, some West African frogs have been known to spontaneously change sex from male to female in a single-sex environment. Malcolm was right...Life found a way."

There is real-life scientific evidence of naturally occurring sex-change in animals, amphibians, and plants (and especially in fish, based on my very top-level Google Scholar search), so this isn't actually a stretch at all in the science of Jurassic Park. While animals and resurrected raptors may demonstrate sex-change to create reproductive value in the ecological system, humans don't necessarily have the same powers by default. We use technology to support our gender alignment, among a host of other things (glasses to support vision, pulleys to support/amplify our strength, clothes for protection and social identity, and on and on). My point here is that 1. the argument that trans people aren't valid because it's "unnatural" simply doesn't hold up to any scrutiny and 2. just because we can't spontaneously change our biological sex like certain fish can doesn't mean that we shouldn't support trans people who socially or medically transition.

Some animals have the ability to change in order to meet their needs. The power of humanity is to create technology to make the changes we need. Sometimes that's changing the technology of clothing to express our gender, sometimes that's changing the environment to be less hostile to the marginalized. Either way, individuals always have and always will make changes, regardless of institutions' attempts to exert control and dominance over them.

Trans people have been under a lot of political turmoil and threats, persecution and endangerment, all because a few people decided to target this vulnerable (and tiny) population to increase their own power and create a distraction for the public to focus on instead of focusing on the authoritarian regimes corroding freedom right now. It's fun to think about Jurassic Park as a trans story where life finds a way to flourish despite arrogant attempts at control, but the real-life implications of our current circumstances are not fun at all. In fact, cisgender women (people who were assigned female at birth and also identify as women), and children (people who can often appear androgynous) are being dragged into the danger because insecure people are frothing at the mouth accusing anyone with a strong jawline, a little bit of height, or cool hairstyles of being transgender. If you just happen to have darker skin , that also correlates to the likelihood you'll be accused of being trans even when you're not—increasing the threat of violence more than what women of color already experience.

Sometimes when we fight so desperately to control other people, all we do is end up hurting ourselves and everyone else. This is one of those moments.

You don't have to be trans to understand that trans people are just people trying to live their lives. I like to think of it this way: if you've ever been misgendered before, you may have felt bad—either embarrassed or awkward or hurt. It's not fun or comfortable to be called something that is wrong. That's what trans people experience, too, but it's all the time, including just seeing a reflection in a mirror. Humans have a social layer built on top of the biological layer, so sometimes it's enough to get rid of or diminish the discomfort and pain of being out of alignment with who you are by simply addressing the social layer: changing your name, your pronouns, and even dressing in a way that expresses your gender. Modern medicine is able to address the deeper layer now, by providing gender-affirming care, allowing humans access to the powers of nature that other species have always had.

There is room for all of us and more. We don't have to understand the trans experience, but I hope that we can tap into empathy more often. Instead of reaching for more power and control over someone else, maybe we can reach for compassion first, and upon realizing that we have more in common, we can abandon or update ideas that were incorrect in the first place.

Always remember humanity. Let life find its way.

item.content:encoded:
There's a very subtle through-line of the 1993 film, Jurassic Park, that sounds eerily relevant in our own technological state of the world, but it's something extremely easy to miss. Let's take a look at a few different scenes throughout the movie, because I think this lays out a pretty accurate history and potential future of technological development and integration with humanity.

The Computer Age

When Dr. Grant, one of the paleontologists, is first introduced to us, he stands up and gruffly mutters, "I hate computers." Dr. Sattler, another paleontologist, immediately quips that "the feeling's mutual," and then escorts him down the hill to take a look at a scrappy machine with a flickering monitor. It's the latest in dinosaur dig-site technology.

"Shoot the radar into the ground and the bone bounces the image back," the computer operator mumbles, explaining while concentrating on his controls and the fuzzy image appearing on the screen.

![[jurassic-park-radar-screen.png]]

"Few more years' development and we won't even have to dig anymore." He continues, typing away while the fossil image gets clearer after a few more passes of rendering.

"Where's the fun in that?" Dr. Grant scowls.

![[jurassic-park-looking-at-raptor-radar-rendering.png]]

Once they can see the dinosaur image, Dr. Sattler and Dr. Grant immediately jump in with their expertise, describing what they see, including guesses on measurements, species (velociraptor), and other features. The screen turns Poltergeist when Dr. Grant gets too close to touching the monitor, and Dr. Sattler explains in yet another quip:

"Dr. Grant's not machine compatible."

"They've got it out for me," Dr. Grant says quietly.

Now we obviously have some funny tension here between these experts and technology. Almost like the scene is pitting them together in a competition to see who is providing more value: the slow humans with expertise? Or the computer programs that are constantly evolving in ways that would essentially take away a huge part of the human paleontologists' work? Grant already is being portrayed as a bit of a curmudgeon in this scene, especially after his little lesson he gives to a kid that doesn't "respect" the velociraptor, calling it a giant turkey.

This is exactly what it probably felt like at the time (1990s) if you were a knowledge worker of some kind, grappling with the new machines that were quickly becoming a daily part of work. There were people who were excited about all of the new possibilities, maybe even making claims that made other people uncomfortable like the computer operator in this scene did with the claim that soon they won't have to dig anymore. There were also people who felt like computers got in the way of their work or were too volatile to rely on. We obviously know what happened since then, because we not only have computers at work, regardless of occupation, and even have computers we put in our pockets for use at all times of the day.

The excavation site scene is very much a grounded, historical take on the technological revolution. It's the implications of the next phase that start to get closer to home in our current situation.

A New World

Fast-forward to Jurassic Park, the incredible realization of technology and biology that pulled dinosaurs out of extinction and into our world. The crew have just seen their first dinosaurs down by the lake. They go into the main building with ultra-rich founder, Dr. Hammond. Walking up the stairs past a giant skeleton of tyrannosaurus rex, Hammond is excitedly babbling about the park and his work:

"...incorporating all the latest technologies in the world...we've made living biological attractions so astounding that they'll capture the imagination of the entire planet."

"So what are you thinking?" Dr. Sattler starts a side conversation.

"That we're out of a job," Dr. Grant replies with a nervous chuckle.

"Don't you mean, 'extinct'?" Dr. Malcolm jabs.

This is such a short moment, it was something I never noticed until after I started writing CYBORG_ and am on the lookout for weird commentary like this. The notion that paleontologists suddenly feel threatened—actually threatened—by technology for their field of work is striking. I see at least these two assumptions baked into Dr. Grant's statement and the context of what the scientists know at this point:

  1. They assume that because they've now seen real biological creatures that those creatures represent the actual dinosaurs from which they were made.
  2. They assume that their contributions and methods are no longer relevant because the creatures are alive.

Granted, they haven't gone on the science-explaining tour just yet at this point in the movie, so they don't know that technically, these dinosaurs are completely new creatures, not resurrected species. I would argue that because the DNA has to be modified by contemporary frog DNA in order to complete the discovered dinosaur DNA sequencing, that the dinosaurs would essentially be a new, created, dinosaur—similar enough, but certainly differing from their ancestors in unexpected ways. Even if this first assumption is true, then the optimist would say that paleontology has not lost any value at all. This actually creates the demand for more paleontology—expanding the field to consider both prehistoric discovery and contemporary biology based on the new living creatures.

In a way this mirrors our real-world knowledge worker situation just a few years ago. The introduction of LLMs to the public invited and required more expertise, because without it, there were gaps that couldn't be bridged. For example, building a custom website is quite hard—ChatGPT could do some of it, maybe even make a cool interface, but when it comes time to put it on a server or maintain it, the gaps become quite difficult to overcome if you have no idea why sharing localhost:8000 doesn't show your website to your friend. .

You could argue that it still didn't really invite more expertise, because companies have made layoffs, claiming AI can now replace those workers. Sometimes this has led to surges of re-hiring for those positions, sometimes not. The thing we can be sure of is that this AI-replacement story is causing volatility in the market. We can also be sure that while experts are less likely to be under threat, it's the entry-level, junior jobs that are getting hit hard right now.

Futures

We get two more moments that continue this question of work for our paleontologist heroes. The next scene is in a tree, where Dr. Grant and the two grandchildren of Dr. Hammond have spent the night.

"What are you and Ellie going to do now if you don't have to pick up dinosaur bones anymore?" Lexie, the oldest, asks.

"I don't know. I guess we'll just have to evolve, too," Dr. Grant answers.

Now, this is technically the last time we actually get a reference to job loss or job transformation. It sounds a lot like what the tech bros are saying: AI is here to stay, and you're going to have to level up—that's how it works. Evolve or die. However, I think it's interesting to add one more moment to complete the thought. At the very end, the kids, Dr. Grant, and Dr. Sattler have reunited. Narrowly escaping the pack of velociraptors, they run to Hammond and Malcom in a Jeep outside the park's visitor center.

"Hammond, after careful consideration, I've decided not to endorse your park," Grant says jumping into the passenger seat."

In miracle of miracles, the old man responds in agreement: "So have I."

I think it is both of these scenes that together help us handle the futures that are ahead of us right now in the world with increasingly better and more dangerous AI. Yes, we'll have to evolve—but that doesn't necessarily mean that we have to accept or adopt AI. It feels too much like accepting a marketing message if the only option is to push forward against all of our better judgment and against our own interests. There are many options available to us, although they may be shrinking.

One option that won't be advertised is Dr. Grant's final conclusion: pushing back against the narrative and not endorsing "the park." In our terms, that might be putting pressure on lawmakers to end the race to AGI/ASI. That might be raising awareness of the dangers that AI poses to everyone. That might be helping your kids avoid and/or navigate this new technology. We may not individually have the influence (or even the chance) to convince an ultra-rich oligarch to stop pursuing destructive and dangerous technology that they have funded, but there is still the possibility that we can collectively be convincing in other ways, especially through regulation.

Jurassic Park offered two predictions for the loss of paleontology as we know it today: first, the computer itself would force them to give up digging for dinosaur bones, and second, the incredible genetic technology of re-creating the dinosaurs themselves would put them to pasture. We don't actually get to see either of these predictions play out. That's because, in my view, it's up to us now to figure out how we want to steer the future. Jobs will be threatened, lives will be up-ended, but I hope we don't stop digging for dinosaur bones, because there is value in slow discovery, in the arts and practices we have participated in anciently, and in understanding our present by better understanding our context within a huge span of evolutionary time. When we lose sight of the past, our future becomes even more tenuous and more easily controlled by a powerful few, rather than a democratic many.

item.content:encoded:
The boom of a kind of bass drum strikes and quickly vibrates away, paired with the rising, unsettling harmony of a small human choir. Silence. Boom again. It is a slow march into the jungle. Trees become visible in the dark atmosphere. Their branches shiver and thrash as though some giant thing is moving towards us.

We finally see humans, all with rapt attention, watching whatever is jostling the trees. A cage emerges, lifted in the air by a fork lift, and is carefully lowered onto a platform. Men with workers' vests and guns surround this ominous delivery. Robert Muldoon, dressed like he's on a safari, barks orders and the others grab onto the cage to push it towards a concrete structure. A snarling creature inside peers out of the dark interior. Everything feels tense, as if on the verge of chaos, but the men proceed to slide the cage into place, a gatekeeper climbs on top of the cage and raises the door.

Shrill squealing punctures the night and the creature's silhouette runs to the back of the cage, slamming it backward. The gatekeeper rolls off as the cage moves violently away from the structure it had been parked at. In a flurry of confusion, men running and shouting, the gatekeeper is dragged towards the cage. He manages to catch himself on the side, but only briefly. Muldoon grabs him, attempting to free the gatekeeper from the grasp of the caged creature and others shove shock prods into the container, trying to subdue what's inside. Amidst the frantic screams and flashes of shocks, the gatekeeper slips through his companion's grasp to his death.

What an initial scene.

If you haven't guessed already, this is from 1993's masterpiece, Jurassic Park. The greatest movie of all time. I'd also submit that it's the greatest AI movie of all time. There's way too much to this movie to unpack in a single article, so I figure it's best to start at the beginning. In just over three minutes, this scene gives us some of the broader themes of AI and human interaction and sets up some of the most important considerations we should be making as we trudge relentlessly towards artificial superintelligence (ASI).

Grown, Not Crafted

I'm currently making my way through the 2025 book, If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies, by Eliezer Yudkowsky and Nate Soares. They easily make a compelling case about the dangers ahead and the logical conclusion that humanity will be wiped out if ASI is ever created (I highly recommend this one!). One line stood out that not only encapsulates the difference between AI and deterministic programming was their heading: Grown, Not Crafted. In earlier phases of digital technology, software was crafted by experts. Sure, there might be flaws or things requiring updates or weird behavior caused by solar flares, but generally speaking what we intended the machine to do was what the machine did. AI, on the other hand, isn't something we've crafted—it's something that is grown. You can't really "program" AI; you can steer it, guide it, but beyond that, there isn't much in the way of control. It is non-deterministic (not determined).

This is where Jurassic Park shines as an effective and understandable metaphor for AI (although, there may be a case for dinosaurs being more than just a metaphor, but that's for another article). The Park is on a secluded island where researchers have cracked the genetic code and have used their technological breakthrough to grow dinosaurs in their lab. From the very first scene, we know a few things: the dinosaurs are alive, strong, and smart.

Throughout the movie, Jurassic Park and its crew cling to the idea of human power and control, as though "nature" is something that can be dominated through sheer force and technology. In fact, the first scene goes out of its way to present safety systems that the park has put into place. We have concrete structures, thick and bold. There is ample lighting despite the nighttime scene. Signs litter the park with warnings in both Spanish and English, alerting people to high-voltage fences and other dangers. The workers have vests and helmets. There are plenty of guns and shock prods to go around. Even Muldoon, the game warden, is giving clear instructions; walking the others through a seemingly well-defined procedure to move the raptor from cage to paddock.

By all accounts, the "safety and security teams" of the park have this little process down. Until the AI—I mean, velociraptor—realizes that it has an opportunity to manipulate its environment to resist being guided into the bigger containment area. Used as an AI metaphor, this is a great example of how safety and security teams are insufficient to control AI and guarantee the safety of the humans interacting with it. They still matter, they're still necessary, but the smarter the AI gets, the more we need other countermeasures and containments. Even with basic AI (not superintelligence, just LLMs), researchers have discovered and demonstrated that the models can "covertly pursue misaligned goals, hiding their true capabilities and objectives" (2). Just the like the raptor, the LLMs can observe and then act in unpredictable ways, despite safety and security measures.

Now, there is a weird space that AI has created for us. We have to remember that it isn't alive in the same sense that we are; it isn't sentient in the same sense that we are; it isn't like us in almost all aspects, despite appearances to the contrary. It can talk as though it has emotions, it can refer to itself, it may even have emergent preferences, but it isn't a poor defenseless creature trapped in a digital cage. Long-time readers will know my stance on this, but it bears repeating. We, humans, are more likely to be deceived into empathizing with AI and seeing it as a being like us than it is to actually become a being like us. That's my opinion, since we can't know something like that for certain, but I would much rather stay skeptical and resistant to the urge to anthropomorphize manipulation machines, because there is no other way to protect real, physical life (see If Anyone Builds It for further exploration on how ASI leads to the demise of human life—if not all life).

So AI, like the dinosaurs of Jurassic Park, are grown, not crafted. You can't craft a life form—parents may try, but eventually their child's agency, preferences, gene expression, environment, social groups, etc. will all have an impact on their behavior and who they will become. AI may not be a life form in the natural sense, but it is non-deterministic, meaning that it isn't programmed or completely controllable or predictable like a deterministic machine is. AI researchers don't even fully understand AI's inner workings. From what I understand, AI's capabilities and behaviors are emergent, based on its training data, its environment, and it likely develops its own preferences and "goals" as part of this process.

Predictable

The opening scene of Jurassic Park tells us exactly what we're going to deal with for the rest of the film: unpredictability in environments that appear controlled. We are used to deterministic programs at this point, because we've had so much experience working with calculators, spreadsheets, word processors, online banking, and even sophisticated SaaS products. Seeing a forklift delivering a large container appears basic. The "creature" (think, something that has been created) inside this delivery seems to have only one choice: go where we are allowing it to go. Instead, it finds another option—one that brings chaos to the humans around it, but does little harm to the creature (and provides a bonus meal).

I think this serves as the perfect representation of our assumptions that AI is just another tool like what we've had before. Sure, we've escorted gorillas and tigers into their pens at a zoo, why would a prehistoric bird-lizard be any different?

The newness of the park plays into this. We humans have had much more experience even now with gorillas and tigers than we ever had with dinosaurs (that is to say, no experience since dinosaurs were extinct before ancient human ancestors emerged). Why would we think that we could control something that our species has never interacted with before? Why should dinosaurs act in the predictable ways that the animals of our current world do?

AI mirror this danger. We have never actually created something that took on its own intelligence and behavior as if it were alive. We've sure thought about the possibility for millennia, playing out ideas in mythology (Hephaestus and his automatons) or exploring it in stories and books (see Frankenstein, for example), but the unpredictability of an entirely new creature—alien to our world in a way—is not so simple. The Park's ultimate warning is as pertinent in its fantastical story as it is in ours: arrogance will be our downfall.

In a scene twenty minutes after the opening, we are met with a reflection of the first scene. A cow is lifted by a crane over the walls of the velociraptor paddock and descends into the lush vegetation. Screams and roars erupt with spine-tingling ferocity and the leaves thrash about violently again. The plants hide the creatures we still haven't seen fully yet (at least as adults), but their sudden movements tell us exactly what is happening. Even Muldoon is there, overseeing the raptors' feeding procedure.

"They should all be destroyed..." Muldoon pronounces as he enters view. Dr. Hammond, the ultra-rich founder of Jurassic Park calls Muldoon an alarmist, even as he introduces him to the crew.

"Alarmist." What a well-selected name to call someone who is interrupting your project. Even if Hammond was the greatest purveyor of altruistic education and research and technological innovation, he still sees this trusted team member as something that suggests "overreaction" and "excessive negativity." Yet, Muldoon sees through the trees, so to speak, to the raptors within. He not only has the experience of dealing with Kenya's wildlife, but has seen what these creatures can do up close and personal—a man was eaten right out from under his grip after all.

Likewise, we may have a similar reaction to people like Yudkowsky and Soares who have written a book whose title is provocatively "alarmist" (If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies). Expert voices like these are also from people who can see through the trees due to their experience in AI research. AI has already played a part in human deaths, and that's without malice, without broader coordination (with other AI models, with systems, etc.), and without superintelligence. It is easy to brush this off and blame the victims for having mental health concerns—humans are the fallible ones, not a machine.

I believe it will take great effort on our part to override our own inclinations to see AI as distinct from deterministic computing. It feels like just a next step in our technological advancement. It feels like AI is something that we control, because we prompt it to do things—unless you're a trusting soul who has allowed an agent to run autonomously on your desktop. Just like a dinosaur in Jurassic Park, however, there are greater dangers than we, the public, can even predict. We have to find a way to snap out of the grand illusion and stop the pursuit of ASI.

This must be a global effort, because we all lose otherwise. Yudkowsky and Soares have made it easy if you're in the U.S. to call your representatives about this issue, including a script for what to say. We can help stop Jurassic Park from being built at all, but we have to act quickly, because the embryos are already viable.

P.S. If you call your reps and get voicemail, you'll need to leave your full address to be counted. If you actually talk to someone on the phone, your zip code is all that's required.

Resources

  1. If Anyone Builds It, Everyone Dies, by Eliezer Yudkowsky & Nate Soares, 2025
  2. Frontier Models are Capable of In-context Scheming, Alexander Meinke, Bronson Schoen, Jérémy Scheurer, Mikita Balesni, Rusheb Shah, Marius Hobbhahn, 2025
  3. The Catastrophic Risks of AI — and a Safer Path, Yoshua Bengio, 2025. TED Talk.

item.dc:creator: Jess Brown
item.content:encoded:
When I have to be somewhere at a certain time, my brain kicks off a very complex system of calculations. When do I need to be there without causing myself social anxiety or embarrassment? I subtract a few minutes from the time I'm told to arrive. How long does it take me to get there? Calculations ensue based on mode of travel, traffic, back roads taken, etc. And a final question: What kind of time-buffer do I need to add so that I'm not stressed in travel?

All of that means that I would reliably arrive outside of my college classrooms 20 minutes prior to class starting. At least as a Freshman—I got much better at wrangling my anxiety, because later it would be just 15 minutes early.

So I'm sitting at a table, waiting to get into an auditorium for a special class that day (I recall it being abnormal, since this wasn't where I usually waited). The doors were open and I could hear the professor's lecture from where I was sitting. He was summarizing a philosophical argument and said something like the following:

"Religion was employed to maintain control over the behavior of the masses. Government can only do so much to determine behavior, but religion—that's a system that drives people from within."

This assertion of institutions exerting either external or internal control was very offensive to me at the time. I remember scowling and thinking of all of my arguments had I the chance to debate this idea. I wasn't religious because I was an unagentic part of the masses. I was above all of that because I had real faith in the real truth. In my defensive reaction, I wasn't able to hear the systemic critique. It wasn't about faith or belief or conviction—it wasn't even about existential "truth." What I missed was what these philosophers were warning about.

I can't remember the professor's actual words, nor can I remember which philosophers he was lecturing on—I don't even know what the class was; it could have been philosophy, political science, or something else. Therefore, I can't unpack specific arguments or references, but from what I remember, the real issue that the professor was taking about was control, and one of the most cogent, real-world attempts at control of the masses right now is in the technology space, specifically through data hoarding and mass surveillance.

To set the stage, I do think that both government and religion broadly can end up using the same technology for the same means (especially when unchecked). The means in question: power and control; the technology: surveillance. In this article, I am using "religion" to refer specifically to American Christianity, since this is the religious system with which I am most familiar (and "religion" is already a word with significant bias towards Protestant Christianity).

Always Observed

My faith tradition instilled an idea that has been extremely difficult for me to work through. From very young, I was told that God was watching me. He could see every action; hear every word; and even know my own thoughts and feelings. Generally, this was supposed to be something comforting. A benevolent God would be able to look upon my heart and know why I misbehaved or said something hurtful or did something I know I shouldn't do.

Perhaps because of my proclivity to anxiety (see timing calculations above), I really took this at face value: there was an all-powerful Being that was constantly observing everything about me. Even though culturally this was intended to be a positive aspect, I felt the other side of this constancy in which judgment was always looming above me like a sword of Damocles. In a way, this teaching interrupted my agency, because I lived in fear of swift punishment that was sure to follow any deviant act, like listening to good music on a Sunday or reading any kind of philosophy or identifying with feminists.

Instead of providing me with comfort and confidence as promised by the messages of a God/Christ who is our advocate, I was trapped in calculations of whether my intentions matched up with my behavior enough, or if I had made enough performances of faith to merit divine favor and avoid punishment or problems. Even scarier is that I was so conditioned to these calculations and the mental weight of knowing I was being watched that I had no idea how much that was wearing down my energy, mental health, and spirit. (Insert plug for therapy here #WorthIt)

Again, I want to reiterate that the critique here is not your personal faith or belief. I'm not interested in determining whether your church or mine or someone else's has a better explanation, method, or doctrine. My neuroses are also my neuroses; my problems are my problems. What's interesting to me is how religion can employ a seemingly simple teaching like "God is watching," to control behavior from within.

A potent example for me is my confusion about feminism. No one told me personally that being upset with misogyny and the systemic oppression of women was a bad thing, but because of the combination of both cultural attitude (anti-feminism) and the application of constant observation created an attitude within me that controlled my behavior despite that behavior being in conflict with my own values. I recall proclaiming that, "Feminism is a bad," to women of my faith who considered themselves feminists. This was my attempt to perform observable behavior in alignment with the faith culture, but in every other way supporting and advocating for women's equality and rights. Instead of being aware of my actual values and beliefs, the feeling of constant observation made me invent ways to appear aligned with external expectations and ignore or justify other behaviors that disagreed with that alignment.

I don't think this is unique to me, because I see similar behavior–value conflicts among friends, family, and even online apologetics. "God is watching" and this is good for those who feel they're in the right (God has validated their behavior and is eagerly awaiting the opportunity to exact justice on "the other"). "God is watching" is bad for those who feel guilty (whether legitimate guilt for wrong-doing or manufactured guilt for humility, anxiety, or any other Christian-flavored motivation for self-abasement).

The technology here is often tied to the surveillance of God (although, perhaps not as consciously as in my case). How else does God know how to judge you in the afterlife? He would have to know what you've done and why. And that kind of data is only gathered through a complete, unbroken view of you, your behavior, your speech, and your thoughts. All of the inner feelings, the doubts, the concerns, the pain, the secret acts, the shame, that you would prefer to stay yours—to stay private—must be accessible and presentable in your celestial court case.

Whether or not a religion is intentionally and consciously attempting to control people and exercise dominion over them, the technology is there at the ready.

Button, Button, Who Has the Button?

As we so often see, religion (especially that Christian flavor we've talked about) blends well into the world of technology. In a way, they are so interrelated for the exact reason that the eavesdropped professor was critiquing: they are attempting to control the masses. Maybe that's with the best of intentions. Tech for a better, safer, healthier, more knowledgable world. Religion for pro-social community-building, inspiring the best of humanity. Religion and tech are trying to make a better world. Sometimes, they are trying to make a utopia, which is, deceptively, not a good place, despite all appearances to the contrary. In the U.S., religion (in principle) is not supposed to be coupled with the power of the state, so technology seems to be taking the place at the seat of power, attempting to do what religion isn't allowed to do: realize the utopian programming.

"Yet these utopians are emblematic of persistent themes in technological discourse today: faith that technology is both the question and the answer, and belief that our machines can bring a perfect world within reach." —God and the Chip: Religion and the Culture of Technology, by William A. Stahl, 1999, page 50-51

There are tech companies (you've likely heard their names a lot recently) whose product is surveillance. The marketing goes like this: What if you lived in a world where there was no crime? Your safety, solved. How? By stopping crime before it happens.

Whether the method is mass surveillance to "find the bad guys" or deep data that can predict when someone is about to commit a crime, the companies all make the same promise that we can get to a world where crime is gone and everyone is safe. It sounds lovely, but rings hollow when you consider the actual cost, and the actual outcome. Near as I can tell, all of these roads lead to authoritarianism. How else do you strip out all privacy? How else do you control enough people? How else do you repeat the same message regardless of evidence to back it up?

Silicon Valley has been pursuing creating a God through artificial intelligence, but from my experience of religion, we've already created a God without requiring super intelligence, because we've created mass surveillance technology. Although in religion, you can at least pray to God and hope for His favor to fall upon you. Private companies that can determine whether you live or die because you fit a profile "enough" despite biases and mistakes is God's constant observation without God's intervention and promise of both justice and mercy.

The more we allow surveillance to have a place in society, the less freedom we have. Not less freedom to commit anti-social crime—that's always available to us—but the freedom to think in alignment with our values; the freedom to challenge assumptions or messages; the freedom to innovate; the freedom to explore. When people and companies talk about safety, but require our data and our privacy to realize that safety, they are not interested in actual safety, they are interested in control.

God is the one with the data and the ability to observe everyone, all the time. God is watching. Who do we want to be our God?

item.content:encoded:
I was ten, sitting on the floor of the basement, three bean bags surrounding me. I had been throwing them and throwing them and throwing them, trying to get them to pass from one hand to the next. I could do jittery circular pattern with two bags, but I wanted to do “real” juggling. I wanted to do the three-ball cascade.

At some point, I realized if I slowed down slightly, threw the bags just a little higher, and passed the bags underneath each other, I could see the pattern emerge. The first time I got something resembling juggling (more than utter chaos), it was euphoric. I was so proud of myself for sticking to this complex task and figuring it out on my own—there was no YouTube at the time to teach me.

Juggling may not be some kind of revolutionary thing—it's quite an old art, actually—but I rarely see women doing it. In fact, it's usually a huge surprise to me to discover a friend can do any kind of juggling pattern. Maybe that's because in my community, girls don't really play with bean bags and balls. I don't think it was overtly discouraged, but it was not encouraged the same way it was with boys, and that's enough to steer some girls away. There's something about juggling that tends to attract boys and men, and I suspect it has to do with upbringing where boys are pushed to explore coordination and sports-like play while girls are left to decide to try that as well. There are other factors, too, like maybe girls still pursue sports, but they keep it to themselves or as a side-passion. As a kid, I never heard a female peer say they wanted to be a professional athlete when they grew up, but quite a few of my male classmates would insist on it.

The other aspect to juggling that suggests this attraction for men is the fact that the highest levels of juggling tournaments are completely dominated by men. Not that men are beating women in these tournaments, but that there are hardly any women participating at all. Luckily, this has been changing, but it still indicates to me that women are being left out of juggling world, probably before they even consider being a part of it. Competition is another one of those things that women aren't really encouraged to do. Don't show off, don't draw too much attention to yourself, don't take away someone else's (i.e. a man's) opportunity to shine.

Delaney Bayles and Other Women You Don't Know

I found a juggling documentary about Delaney Bayles last year and I was deeply inspired by her story, which starts in the early 2000s, contemporaneous to my own private juggling journey. Bayles started entering tournaments and at one of her first, she recalls that the host gave her an honorable mention "for being the only woman in the competition."

...it didn't sit well with me and I was like, next time they call my name, it's going to be because I won and not because I'm a woman. And I don't think I have to tell you who won that competition next year. —Bayles, Timestamp: 8:24

I won't be able to tell her story as well as the documentary, so I definitely recommend watching it! What I find most relevant to CYBORG_ is how the technology of gender can be employed in such fragile ways, to the point that we, the world, miss out on the greatest talent, skill, invention, creativity, and potential just because of rigid gender expectations.

To think that even in the 2000s, Bayles could be the only female in a competition is just flooring to me. Especially because, in my view, the sport of juggling doesn't have any biological advantages based on sex assigned at birth. A man has no special advantage over a woman for any form of juggling as far as I can tell, so why the drastic deficit of representation?

Fast forward to 2024, and the International Jugglers' Association (IJA) releases this International Women's Day Collaboration Video. Featuring over 100 women jugglers, this video is an awesome, entertaining, and impressive compilation. There was diversity I had not seen before (in juggling) all in one place: cis and trans women; very young girls and older women; professional and amateur. When I saw this, I was astounded, but it was the ending that made me choke back tears. A cold room with what looks like concrete walls adorned with cracked paint—perhaps an underfunded school—full of kids, all juggling, shouting, "Happy Women's Day!" intermittently.

Maybe it's my proximity to juggling, but there's something about seeing kids and especially more women practicing and showing off their juggling. To me, juggling represents my curiosity and dedication to learning complex movement patterns. It is a method of self-soothing when I'm stressed or anxious. It is the hope I clung to when I started recovering from my MS attack and lost my coordination for months. It represents a kind of rebellion—it's a sport, but not a sport because it can be whatever you want it to be; it can be performed by people you expect and people you don't expect.

When I see women taking up juggling, I see the world moving in a better direction—more exploratory, more inclusive, more space to move and grow and do. It's not the solution to the world's many problems, but it feels like an indicator of change. After all, it's sometimes the small things that predict or create larger changes. If the victory is just getting kids back into the physical world while they play, it's worth it. If the victory is a 50 year-old mom deciding to try something totally new, it's worth it. If the victory is a woman having the confidence to shakily perform the "basic" three-ball cascade and show off to someone else, it's worth it.

In a world that is trying to keep women out of sports, police women's bodies, and define what a woman is and who gets to be counted as one, I see juggling as the kind of potential space of radical inclusion necessary to stand in contrast.

item.dc:creator: Jess Brown
item.content:encoded:
Few historical characters pervaded my imagination more as a kid than Leonardo Da Vinci. I have always insisted on occupying the awkward space of creativity and science (made awkward only by social constructions), and Da Vinci seemed like my kind of guy. He displayed an array of skills and interests that involved the combination of science, art, geometry, invention, engineering, encryption, etc. It was exactly that kind of exploratory, forever-student model that drew me towards his work and still catches my attention today.

Learning about Da Vinci sporadically throughout my life, one of the things I've been consistently interested in are his drawings and notes found in what's called a codex. To me, looking through Da Vinci's codices at the V&A museum website is one of the great joys of modern technology. This unique combination of digital technology and ancient technology (the codex) has gotten me thinking about the differences, the properties, and missed opportunities of over-investing in the digital space for things like learning and research.

My biggest question as a web developer is: why does the web seem to fall short compared to books for things like learning and research? Before we can try to answer this question, let's first talk about what a codex is and why it's so flipping cool.

The Codex

I first recall hearing about a "codex" because of Leornardo Da Vinci. There are several famous codices that he produced, like the Forster Codices, that show off inventions and ideas and even contain the encrypted writing style that Da Vinci is famous for: writing upside-down and backwards. Because of the fame of these works and the sense of mystery that Da Vinci inspires, I assumed that "codex" meant something like "code." Something cool, secretive, or difficult to understand. In reality, "codex" is the earlier root from which "code" evolves, and more importantly, it refers to the kind of binding that creates the book itself. So Forster Codex I isn't a reference to the Da Vinci mirror writing or some sort of abstracted puzzle to be worked out, it's a reference to the binding of the book that collects all of the pages together.

A book that I pull off the shelf at home or at a library is most likely a codex. It binds several loose-leaf pages ("folios") and then multiple sets of folios ("signatures") are sewn together at the spine of the book. Usually we don't call books codices anymore, because that's basically become coupled with terminology for ancient pieces like the Da Vinci codices or scripture like Codex Sinaiticus, but the technology itself is essentially the same (at least as far as I understand it, see notes below for sources).

Why is this so important? I think that books have become so ubiquitous and commonplace that we've forgotten that they are actual technology, and therefore have unique features and properties that we may not realize are available to us. For example, as described by the entry for codex in the Encyclopedia Britannica:

"The codex had several advantages over the roll, or scroll. It could be opened at once to any point in the text, it enabled one to write on both sides of the leaf, and it could contain long texts."

Two important things we can pull out from that quote for this discussion:

  1. The advantages described are features of the technology of books.
  2. The scroll was a predecessor to the codex—interesting to keep this in mind when we move back to the web where scrolling is one of the most common actions.

If we look at what a book offers to us in terms of its interface and features, we can see that books still give us certain advantages today. If I'm reading a book and find an interesting reference, I can hold my place with a bookmark or just a finger, flip to the back and get more context from the endnotes or the index, before going back to continue at the part I was reading. On the web, we have a similar experience where we can open a link in a new tab and quickly flip back and forth. Arguably, linking together references is the strong point of the web, and in my view, the entire reason for the success of the Internet.

The Internet is based on the idea of documents bound together. Every webpage is a file (at least originally; there are tricks that aren't quite so straightforward, depending on the code framework). In a way, a website is kind of like a codex for multiple scrolls where links are both the binding for the website and also the threads that you can follow to other websites. While an ancient scroll could barely contain a short text like the Book of Matthew from the New Testament, and a codex could eventually contain the entire Bible, the Internet is practically unlimited in what it can bind together (Brittanica).

It already seems like the digital space is set to outpace books in every way, but if we continue to compare the experience of reading in a book to reading online or on digital devices, some advantages really start to shine.

A distinct advantage of books is in leveraging our brains' location-based memory. Since a book is a fixed layout—meaning that it's not going to change because you've turned the book on its side or left it for a while and web developers have made adjustments in your absence—we can often better remember where to find passages or information based simply on its relative location. There are books I've read so frequently that I know to look on the top-left column, a few lines down to find what I'm looking for. Knowing that my passage is towards the end of the book, I just have to look for the layout that matches my location-based memory. It's like having a multi-layered map both in memory and in print, where the larger location is the rough part of the book (beginning, middle, end) and then we can drill down to the specifics (it's in Chapter X at the one page that had a picture).

A website, in contrast, is likely to break your location-based memory pattern, especially if the content is highly volatile, like on marketing websites or, even worse, social media platforms. As design trends come and go, people rebuild their templates in ways that make it impossible to rely on pattern recognition to find what you've found before. Sometimes, against good practice, website updates also destroy or move around the URL structure, causing SEO headaches, but also breaking your own mental model of the site if you were a frequent visitor.

Distractions are possible for both physical and digital media, but unfortunately, most digital interfaces are designed with distractions as a part of the experience. Books are only subject to distractions external to it (your environment, your focus), while most digital spaces, apps, or websites contain internal distractions, tempting you to surf, change to something else, or pull attention toward ads or notifications.

There are more features to explore, but the final one to consider for now is the experience. All of my career, I've heard the exact same request when building some new webpage or website. We want a unique, intriguing experience! Designers, marketers, and web developers are all desperately looking for ways to make their content really cool and engaging, but it never quite gets there. To be sure, there are plenty of cool websites out there. We add colors, images, interactive elements, and animations all in the hopes that we can turn our boring old website content into something that people want to read (note that this is distinct from social media platforms, where addictive design is implemented—you don't get the same staying power from a marketing website).

What is missing from the web, then? In terms of learning and understanding content, why does the web fall short?

Computers vs. Books

In a scene from Buffy the Vampire Slayer—you saw this reference coming, right?!—Mr. Giles, the librarian is talking to Ms. Calendar about computers. Giles is frequently depicted in conflict with digital technology throughout the series, but especially in the first few seasons.

"Honestly, what is it about [computers] that bothers you so much?" Ms. Calendar asks.

"The smell," Giles says definitively.

"Computers don't smell, Rupert." She responds.

"I know. Smell is the most powerful trigger to the memory there is...Books smell; musty and rich. The knowledge gained from a computer is...it has no texture, no context, it's there and then it's gone. If it's to last then, the getting of knowledge should be tangible; it should be smelly."

Maybe Giles is on to something. In the digital space, there is a lack of texture—a lack of engagement of almost all of the senses. Books and physical media can activate our entire sensory experience (apart from taste...although babies and children still get that aspect, ha!). "Physical" reading is an experiential interface that can't be replicated on a screen.

I think that this scene also perfectly illustrates the tension between the physical and the digital forms of knowledge collection and dissemination, but I also think it's too easy to assume that we must abandon one form of technology for another. Perhaps this was the concern of the generation in the 1990s/early 2000s when Buffy was created. Now, what we face is more complex. There are undeniable advantages that computers and especially the Internet have brought to humanity. Accessibility being the primary one in my mind. Computers and especially smart phones have given people in the farthest reaches of the earth the ability to access information that would be impossible relying solely on physical print materials. Yes, of course, there are still places that can't actually reach the Internet due to connection or access to the devices or cultural choices to abstain from modern technology. However, the Internet is still in large part more accessible than something like libraries are at the global scale.

I can't argue that the answer is to assume that digital technology offers no worthwhile learning opportunities. I've learned coding principles from YouTubers that are sometimes better explained and taught than at MIT computer science classes (I've seen some of those on YouTube, too). I've learned about social issues and studies from creators that have literally changed my life, inspired my own research for this newsletter, and helped me find space to live authentically, all of which would have been impossible without the digital realm.

What I think is the better question than who would win in an intellectual fight: a book or a computer? is the question of usefulness: Which medium will serve me best given my current goal?

This is a question we don't ask—at least not that I can tell. In the discussion of books vs. the Internet is the assumption that both provide the same thing, and therefore the winner becomes a matter of preference or habit. However, technology is not neutral. That includes the design, the motivations, the incentives, the intended use, and the actual use of technology. A book can be awful and damaging (see Ann Coulter's works, which filled my head for too long with lies and racist apologetics). A book can also break down damaging frameworks and provide hope or inspire real change. So too, can a YouTube channel or a website or a digital medium hold both constructive and destructive information. The content of a technology, therefore, is also not necessarily a measure of usefulness.

Offloading vs. Instilling

In my experience spending decades trying to learn design and build compelling websites, I've come to realize that imitating books online will simply fail (have you ever been to a magazine "experience" on the web where it animates flipping the page? It's deeply annoying to me, at least). The web is a new medium, and therefore it breaks from its predecessors to provide different advantages and disadvantages.

In terms of discovery, digital media seem to be especially well-suited for wide exploration. AI can help us sort through the infinite expanse of information to find things we are looking for, but also things that we've never seen or heard of before. I also see digital media as a great way for distilling or offloading information. For example with CYBORG_, I find the act of content creation to be very fulfilling and also a great use of my web-publishing skills. I'm currently working on a timeline that will help me distill all of the references I've used in these articles that also puts them in historical and social context (the page is very work-in-progress, but you get a preview!). It's been a long time since we've talked about personal knowledge management (PKM) tools like Obsidian, but those are also excellent ways of offloading knowledge and quotes and references. PKM tools use the powers inherent to the web / digital media to make connections, help you surf your own curated "internet," and can be a great way to learn from what you've already decided is valuable.

Reading in a book offers a different experience—one of instilling rather than offloading. It is usually slower and more focused. The practice also seems to help us internalize new information, whether that's thoughts and ideas or empathy for others. You can go deeper with books, especially since deep research online often contains barriers like pay-walls that prevent you from easily accessing information. Libraries are also a part of the experience of physical media in my view. They add the experience of moving through physical space—again, triggering location-based memory—and often providing the means to get around some paywalls.

The slowness and the depth that reading from an actual book has many benefits, but I especially like how Maryanne Wolf sums it up here:

There are many things that would be lost if we slowly lose the cognitive patience to immerse ourselves in the worlds created by books and the lives and feelings of the "friends" who inhabit them. And although it is a wonderful thing that movies and film can do some of this too, there is a difference in the quality of immersion that is made possible by entering the articulated thoughts of others. What will happen to young readers who never meet and begin to understand the thoughts and feelings of someone totally different? What will happen to older readers who begin to lose touch with that feeling of empathy for people outside their ken or kin? It is a formula for unwitting ignorance, fear, and misunderstanding that can lead to the belligerent forms of intolerance that are the opposite of America's original goals for its citizens of many cultures. —Reader Come Home, chapter 3, transcribed starting at 01:29:45.

I think our best future is served when we stop assuming that technology is all the same. Books are well-suited for some goals, websites for others. Even more concerning is the loss of readership and literacy in society as we default more and more to short-form, interruptive content and videos. Examining our media habits may be one of the most important exercises that we can do.

For me, code is how I distill my thoughts, find what I've found before, explore, and entertain, but when I want to connect, grow, understand, and touch base with humanity, I'll go to codex. Thanks for reading with me.

Notes and Resources

Agassi, Ido. This is the most entrancing and chill YouTube channel on the entire Internet. He is a master craftsman, book-binder, box-maker. Consider the half-binding project he demonstrates to see the book binding process and how books can be held together. There are many techniques and variant designs, but this is ultimately the idea of the codex: binding multiple loose-leaf pages together into a single collection.

Allen, Roland. The Notebook: A History of Thinking on Paper. 2024. This book is a one-of-a-kind compilation of the history of notebooks: how we got from mark-making on durable, but less manageable, materials like stone and wood to wax-tablets to the eventual invention of paper and finally to the notebook. One of my favorite, fascinating resources that I keep coming back to.

Britannica Editors. "codex." Encyclopedia Britannica, June 5, 2026. https://www.britannica.com/topic/codex-manuscript, accessed 8/9/2026. A quick overview of the codex. "The codex had several advantages over the roll, or scroll. It could be opened at once to any point in the text, it enabled one to write on both sides of the leaf, and it could contain long texts."

Wolf, Maryanne. Reader Come Home: The Reading Brain in a Digital World. 2018. I'm still working my way through this book, but it is an excellent look at the neuroscience involved in reading and how reading impacts us.
